lessons.title: Selecting Breeding Stock
lessons.body: Selecting the right breeding stock is the foundation of a profitable turkey farm. Start by choosing birds that are healthy, vigorous, and free from deformities. In Africa, local breeds like the indigenous turkey are hardy and disease-resistant, but they may grow slower. For meat production, consider crossbreeds such as the Norfolk Black or Bronze. Look for broad-breasted birds with strong legs, as they must support heavy weight during mating. Select hens that lay regularly and have a calm temperament; aggressive hens may injure chicks. For toms (males), choose those with a large, upright fan, bright caruncles, and active strutting behavior. Avoid birds with crooked keels, slipped wings, or pasty vents. A good rule: select from parents that have a proven record of high hatchability and fast growth. In Africa, where feed costs are high, prioritize feed efficiency. Weigh birds at 16-20 weeks; keep those above average weight. Keep a ratio of 1 tom to 8-10 hens to ensure fertile eggs without overworking males. Buy stock from reputable hatcheries or established farmers, not from live bird markets where disease risk is high. Quarantine new birds for 3 weeks before mixing. Record the source, age, and performance of each bird. Cull any bird that shows signs of illness, poor growth, or low egg production. Remember, good genetics plus good management equals success. Start with 10-20 hens and 2-3 toms for a small-scale farm. Over time, replace older birds (after 2-3 years) with their best offspring to maintain vigor.

lessons.title: Mating Systems
lessons.body: Mating systems determine how you pair toms and hens to produce the next generation. The simplest is pen mating: keep 1 tom with 8-10 hens in a confined area. This works well for small farms but can lead to inbreeding if you keep related birds. To avoid this, rotate toms every 2 years or bring in new blood. Another system is flock mating, where multiple toms run with a larger flock. This mimics natural mating but you cannot control which tom fathers which poults. For genetic improvement, use artificial insemination (AI). AI allows you to use one superior tom to fertilize many hens, and it prevents injuries from heavy toms mounting hens. In Africa, AI is gaining popularity because it reduces the number of males needed. To collect semen, train the tom to mount a dummy or a hen, then massage the vent. Collect 0.2-0.5 ml per ejaculation, dilute with saline, and inseminate hens within 30 minutes. Inseminate each hen every 7-10 days. For natural mating, ensure the pen floor is not slippery; provide deep litter (wood shavings or sand) to prevent leg injuries. Watch for over-mating: hens with bare backs or wounds need rest. Separate them for a week. Rotate breeding groups every 6 months to maintain fertility. If you keep a tom for more than 2 years, fertility drops. Replace him with a young, vigorous tom. Always keep records of which tom mated which hens so you can trace parentage. In hot climates, mate in early morning or evening to avoid heat stress. Provide fresh water and shade. A good mating system balances genetic diversity, fertility, and bird welfare.

lessons.title: Egg Production and Management
lessons.body: A healthy turkey hen lays 60-100 eggs per year, mostly between 30 and 54 weeks of age. In Africa, egg production can be lower due to heat and poor nutrition. To maximize egg numbers, provide a laying diet with 16-18% protein and 3-4% calcium. Use crushed oyster shells or limestone as calcium sources. Hens need 14-16 hours of light daily; if natural daylight is short, use a bulb (40 watts per 20 square meters) to extend light. Collect eggs at least 3 times a day to prevent breakage and dirty eggs. Nest boxes should be dark, clean, and lined with soft bedding like dry grass. One nest box per 4-5 hens. Eggs for hatching should be stored at 15-18Â°C and 75% humidity for no more than 7 days. Turn them twice daily if stored longer. Do not wash hatching eggs; instead, gently wipe with a dry cloth. If eggs are dirty, use a fine sandpaper. In hot climates, store eggs in a cool room or evaporative cooler. Never store eggs near strong smells like kerosene or onions, as they absorb odors. Keep a record of lay: date, number of eggs, and any abnormalities. Soft-shelled or thin-shelled eggs indicate calcium deficiency or disease. If a hen lays outside the nest, confine her to the nest box for a few days. Broody hens stop laying; if you want eggs, break broodiness by moving the hen to a wire-bottom cage for 3-5 days. For hatching, select eggs that are well-shaped, average size, and free of cracks. Discard very small or double-yolked eggs. With good management, you can get 70-80% fertile eggs and 60-70% hatchability.

lessons.title: Incubation and Hatching
lessons.body: Turkey eggs take 28 days to hatch. You can use a natural hen (a broody turkey or chicken) or an incubator. For small flocks, a broody hen is cheap and effective. Set 8-12 eggs under a broody hen at night. She will turn them and keep them warm. Provide her with food and water nearby. For larger scale, use a forced-air incubator. Set temperature at 37.5Â°C (99.5Â°F) and humidity at 55-60% for the first 25 days. Then increase humidity to 70-80% for the last 3 days (lockdown). Turn eggs at least 5 times a day, or use an automatic turner. Stop turning on day 25. Candle eggs on day 7 and day 14 to remove infertile or dead embryos. Infertile eggs look clear; dead embryos show a blood ring. Remove them to prevent contamination. In Africa, power outages are common. Use a backup generator or a solar-powered incubator. If power fails, wrap the incubator in blankets and do not open it for up to 2 hours. After hatching, leave poults in the incubator until they are dry and fluffy (12-24 hours). Then move them to a brooder with a heat source (infrared lamp or charcoal stove) at 35Â°C for the first week, reducing by 3Â°C each week. Provide clean water with vitamins and a starter feed of 28% protein. Dip beaks in water to teach drinking. Keep bedding dry. Hatch rate depends on egg quality, incubation hygiene, and temperature control. Sanitize incubator before and after each hatch. With practice, you can achieve 80% hatch of fertile eggs.

lessons.title: Genetic Improvement
lessons.body: Genetic improvement means selecting the best birds to breed so that each generation is better than the last. Start by defining your goal: do you want faster growth, more eggs, or better disease resistance? In Africa, disease resistance and heat tolerance are often more important than maximum growth. Choose a selection method. Individual selection: pick birds based on their own performance (e.g., weight at 20 weeks). Family selection: pick birds whose parents and siblings also perform well. This is better for traits like egg production. For growth, weigh birds at 8, 16, and 24 weeks. Keep the heaviest 20% as breeders. For egg production, count eggs per hen from 30 to 45 weeks. Keep hens that lay above average. Use a breeding card for each bird: record ID, hatch date, weight, eggs laid, and health. Avoid inbreeding by not mating close relatives (father-daughter, brother-sister). Introduce new blood every 3-4 years from a different farm or hatchery. Crossbreeding can give hybrid vigor: cross two different breeds (e.g., local hen with Broad Breasted White tom) to get faster-growing offspring. But keep pure lines if you want to sell breeding stock. In hot climates, select for smaller body size and good feed conversion. Cull aggressively: any bird with deformities, poor growth, or chronic illness should not breed. Over time, you can improve growth by 5-10% per generation. Keep records for at least 3 generations to see trends. Join a farmer group to exchange breeding stock and ideas. Remember, genetic improvement is slow but permanent. Good nutrition and health unlock genetic potential.

lessons.title: Record Keeping for Breeding
lessons.body: Record keeping is the backbone of a successful breeding program. Without records, you cannot know which birds are performing well. Start with a simple notebook or a spreadsheet on a phone. For each bird, assign a unique ID (e.g., leg band or wing tag). Record: hatch date, sex, parent IDs, weight at 8, 16, and 24 weeks, date of first egg, number of eggs laid per week, egg weight, fertility, hatchability, and health treatments. For mating, record which tom was with which hens and dates. For incubation, record set date, number of eggs set, candling results, hatch date, and number of poults hatched. Use a calendar to track dates. In Africa, where many farmers operate without electricity, use a chalkboard or a waterproof notebook. Keep records in a safe, dry place. At the end of each season, calculate key figures: average eggs per hen, fertility rate (fertile eggs / eggs set), hatch rate (poults hatched / fertile eggs), and growth rate (weight gain per day). Compare these to previous seasons. Identify your best 10% of birds and use them as breeders next year. Cull the bottom 20%. Share records with buyers to prove quality. For example, a buyer will pay more for poults from a hen that lays 90 eggs per year than from one that lays 50. Records also help you spot problems early: a drop in fertility may mean a tom is too old or overheated. A drop in egg production may mean disease or poor feed. Keep records for at least 3 years to see genetic trends. Train your workers to record daily. Use simple codes: 'E' for egg, 'H' for hatched, 'D' for dead. Good records turn a hobby into a business.

quiz.q: What is the recommended ratio of toms to hens in a breeding pen?
quiz.explanation: A ratio of 1 tom to 8-10 hens ensures good fertility without overworking the male.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a sign of a good breeding tom?
quiz.explanation: A large, upright fan indicates a healthy, vigorous tom.

quiz.q: How long should new breeding birds be quarantined before mixing with the flock?
quiz.explanation: A 3-week quarantine helps prevent the spread of diseases.

quiz.q: What is a disadvantage of pen mating?
options: B) It can lead to inbreeding
C) It cannot be used in small farms
quiz.explanation: Keeping related birds together in a pen can lead to inbreeding depression.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of artificial insemination in turkeys?
options: A) It is cheaper than natural mating
B) It allows one superior tom to fertilize many hens
D) It eliminates the need for records
quiz.explanation: AI maximizes the use of genetically superior males and reduces injury to hens.

quiz.q: How often should you inseminate a hen for good fertility?
quiz.explanation: Inseminating every 7-10 days maintains high fertility in turkey hens.

quiz.q: What is the ideal protein level in a laying turkey diet?
quiz.explanation: Laying hens need 16-18% protein for good egg production.

quiz.q: How many hours of light per day do turkey hens need for maximum egg production?
quiz.explanation: 14-16 hours of light stimulates laying.

quiz.q: What should you do with dirty hatching eggs?
options: B) Wipe gently with a dry cloth
quiz.explanation: Washing removes the protective bloom; gentle wiping is safer.

quiz.q: What is the storage temperature for hatching eggs?
quiz.explanation: 15-18Â°C is ideal for short-term storage of hatching eggs.

quiz.q: What is the incubation period for turkey eggs?
quiz.explanation: Turkey eggs take 28 days to hatch.

quiz.q: What is the correct temperature for a forced-air incubator during the first 25 days?
quiz.explanation: 37.5Â°C (99.5Â°F) is the standard temperature for turkey egg incubation.

quiz.q: When should you stop turning eggs in the incubator?
quiz.explanation: Turning stops on day 25 to allow the poult to position for hatching.

quiz.q: What does a clear egg at candling on day 7 indicate?
quiz.explanation: Clear eggs are infertile and should be removed.

quiz.q: What is the recommended brooder temperature for poults in the first week?
quiz.explanation: 35Â°C is needed for day-old poults, reducing by 3Â°C each week.

quiz.q: What is the protein level for turkey starter feed?
quiz.explanation: Turkey poults need 28% protein starter for rapid growth.

quiz.q: Which selection method is best for improving egg production?
quiz.explanation: Family selection considers relatives' performance, which is better for low-heritability traits like egg number.

quiz.q: How often should you introduce new blood into a breeding flock to avoid inbreeding?
quiz.explanation: Introducing new blood every 3-4 years maintains genetic diversity.

quiz.q: What is hybrid vigor?
options: A) The superior performance of crossbred offspring
quiz.explanation: Hybrid vigor is the improved performance of crossbreds over purebreds.

quiz.q: What percentage of the heaviest birds should you keep as breeders for growth improvement?
quiz.explanation: Selecting the top 20% for growth gives the best genetic gain.

quiz.q: Why is record keeping important in breeding?
options: A) To know which birds perform best
C) To make the farm look busy
quiz.explanation: Records identify top performers for selection and culling.

quiz.q: What is a simple method for identifying individual birds?
options: A) Leg bands or wing tags
quiz.explanation: Leg bands or wing tags provide unique IDs for each bird.

quiz.q: What does a fertility rate measure?
options: B) Fertile eggs divided by eggs set
C) Poults hatched divided by eggs set
quiz.explanation: Fertility rate is the percentage of set eggs that are fertile.

quiz.q: How long should you keep breeding records?
quiz.explanation: At least 3 years of records are needed to see genetic trends.

quiz.q: What is a sign that a tom may be infertile?
quiz.explanation: A drop in fertility often indicates an old or overheated tom.

quiz.q: What should you do with a broody hen if you want her to continue laying?
options: A) Leave her on the nest
B) Move her to a wire-bottom cage for 3-5 days
quiz.explanation: Moving to a wire-bottom cage breaks broodiness and restarts laying.

quiz.q: What is the ideal humidity for the first 25 days of incubation?
quiz.explanation: 55-60% humidity is correct for the first 25 days; it increases to 70-80% for lockdown.

quiz.q: What is the best way to teach poults to drink?
options: A) Wait for them to find water
B) Dip their beaks in water
quiz.explanation: Dipping beaks in water ensures each poult learns to drink immediately.

quiz.q: Which trait is most important for turkey breeding in hot African climates?
quiz.explanation: Heat tolerance is crucial for survival and production in hot climates.

quiz.q: What is the first step in a genetic improvement program?
quiz.explanation: You must know what you want to improve before selecting birds.
